title: Wheels and Chassis
description: Component lesson. A motor's spin has to turn into travel, and travel has to be carried by something. Two more parts, both simpler than they look.

content.value: A wheel converts spinning into distance. Every time it completes one full rotation, the robot travels exactly one circumference forward — a fixed, calculable distance that depends only on the wheel's diameter.

circumference = π × diameter

ARIA's wheel: 6.5 cm diameter
circumference = π × 6.5 ≈ 20.4 cm per rotation

10 rotations ≈ 204 cm travelled

A bigger wheel covers more ground per rotation, which means faster travel for the same motor RPM — but also less torque available to get moving, since the motor's turning force is now acting on a longer lever arm. Wheel size is a real design trade-off, not just a cosmetic choice.
The Chassis: More Than a Base Plate

The chassis is the structural frame every other part mounts to — battery, controller, motors, sensors. Its job sounds passive, but where weight sits on it matters enormously. A robot with its centre of mass too high, or too far forward, can tip during a sharp turn or an abrupt stop, the same way a top-heavy shopping trolley tips on a fast corner.
ARIA's design keeps the heaviest single part — the battery — mounted low and central, which is a deliberate choice: it lowers the centre of mass and keeps weight balanced between both drive wheels.

A three-point base (two driven wheels plus one caster) is inherently stable on any reasonably flat surface — three points always define a plane, which is exactly why you'll see this layout on nearly every beginner robot, including ARIA.
Key takeaway: a wheel's circumference sets exactly how far one rotation carries the robot. A chassis's job is structural, and where weight sits on it directly affects stability.

quiz.question: ARIA's wheel has a 6.5 cm diameter. Roughly how far does she travel in one full wheel rotation?
quiz.explain: Circumference = π × diameter ≈ 3.14 × 6.5 ≈ 20.4 cm — one rotation, one circumference of travel.

quiz.question: What's the trade-off of fitting larger-diameter wheels to the same motor?
options: No trade-off — bigger is always better
Faster travel per rotation, but less torque available to get moving
Slower travel per rotation, but more torque
quiz.explain: A bigger wheel covers more ground per turn (speed) but acts as a longer lever arm against the motor's turning force (less effective torque).

quiz.question: Why does ARIA's design keep the battery mounted low and central on the chassis?
options: It has nothing to do with stability, just convenience
It lowers the centre of mass and balances weight between both drive wheels, reducing tipping risk
quiz.explain: Where weight sits on the chassis directly affects how easily the robot tips during sharp turns or stops — low and central is the stable choice.
